screens.title: Essential Command-Line Troubleshooting Tools
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll make the command line your most reliable troubleshooting partner. The tools covered here are small, fast, and available on nearly every machine: ping for basic reachability and latency, traceroute or tracert to see the path packets take, ipconfig or ifconfig to inspect local interface settings, netstat to reveal active connections and listening ports, and nslookup or dig to validate DNS resolution. You will learn not only how to run these tools but how to read their outputs and combine them into a stepwise diagnostic approach. For example, you might start by pinging a public IP to verify basic connectivity, then run nslookup if a hostname fails, and finally use tracert to find a broken hop. These utilities give you immediate clues about source vs. resolver vs. path problems. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to pick the right command for the symptom, interpret typical outputs, and avoid common mistakes like assuming a timeout always means the host is down. Think of these tools as quick mental checks that point you where to look next.

screens.title: ping — verify reachability and measure latency
screens.narratorSegment: Ping is the most basic test for IP-level reachability. It sends ICMP Echo Request packets to a target and waits for Echo Replies. A successful sequence of replies tells you the host is reachable at the IP level and gives you round-trip times that show latency and packet loss percentages. For example, the sample ping to 192.168.1.1 returns four replies with 1 millisecond round trip times and zero packet loss; that confirms local connectivity to the gateway. A 'Request timed out' can mean several things: the host is down, an intermediate device is dropping ICMP, or a firewall blocks echo replies. That is an important misconception to avoid — a timeout does not always mean the device has failed. Use ping first to a known-good public IP such as 8.8.8.8 to test general internet reachability. If that works but ping to a hostname fails, combine this with nslookup to separate DNS from connectivity problems. As a closing thought, always treat ping as a quick snapshot: it confirms reachability at that moment and points you to the next test, not as a final verdict.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › ping — verify reachability
Definition
What ping does
Ping sends ICMP Echo Request packets and listens for Echo Replies. It reports replies, round-trip times, and packet loss statistics so you can verify IP-level connectivity and latency.
Common outputs and what they mean
  • Reply lines with times indicate successful reachability and measured latency.
  • Packet loss in statistics reveals reliability issues between hosts.
  • Request timed out can mean ICMP is blocked or the host is unreachable — follow up is required.
Key Takeaway

Use ping as your first reachability check, then combine with DNS or route checks when results are ambiguous.

Example — Windows output
C:\Users\User>ping 192.168.1.1

Pinging 192.168.1.1 with 32 bytes of data:
Reply from 192.168.1.1: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=64
Reply from 192.168.1.1: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=64
Reply from 192.168.1.1: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=64
Reply from 192.168.1.1: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=64

Ping statistics for 192.168.1.1:
    Packets: Sent = 4, Received = 4, Lost = 0 (0% loss),
Approximate round trip times in milli-seconds:
    Minimum = 1ms, Maximum = 1ms, Average = 1ms
Concrete scenario: if your gateway replies quickly with no loss, focus on application-layer checks. If ping to the gateway fails, check cables, link lights, and ipconfig for interface state before proceeding.

screens.title: Reading ping statistics: latency, loss, TTL
screens.narratorSegment: When you review ping output, focus on three measurable signals: round-trip time, packet loss, and the TTL value. Round-trip time indicates latency between your host and the target; consistently high numbers point to congestion or long paths. Packet loss in the summary shows reliability: any consistent loss implies packets are being dropped somewhere between sender and receiver and often leads to application problems. TTL, while not a latency metric, can help differentiate local versus remote devices: lower TTL values typically come from farther hops; sudden large TTL changes are a clue you're hitting different network segments. A common misconception is to treat a single slow reply as definitive; transient fluctuations can occur. Look for consistent patterns across multiple ping packets. Use ping first to an IP you trust, such as a gateway or a public DNS, to decide whether to escalate to traceroute. For example, if ping to 8.8.8.8 shows 0% loss but high latency only during business hours, suspect congestion; if loss appears to a single hop, run traceroute to find where loss or timeouts begin. Reading ping statistics: latency, loss, TTL means ping gives you a brief snapshot of latency and reliability; interpret trends not single samples and follow up when results are ambiguous.. In practical terms, what round-trip time, packet loss, and ttl tell you about network health. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Reading ping statistics
Interpretation guide
  • Round-trip time: Consistently high values suggest latency on the path; compare to expected local values.
  • Packet loss: Any non-zero persistent loss indicates dropped packets and a reliability problem.
  • TTL: Time-to-live helps infer distance in hops; surprising TTL values can mean different routing or NAT behavior.
Concrete example: if you ping a gateway and get 1ms with 0% loss, the LAN is healthy. If you ping a public IP and see 30–100 ms and occasional loss, suspect upstream congestion or ISP issues. If every ping times out to a host, try pinging the gateway and then a public IP to narrow whether the issue is local or beyond.
Common mistake
Assuming a single timeout means the server is down. It can be ICMP filtering or transient loss.
Pro tip
Ping multiple targets and at different times to determine if the problem is persistent or transient.
Quick checklist
  • Ping the gateway; if it fails, check interface configuration.
  • Ping a public IP like 8.8.8.8 to test Internet reachability.
  • Compare ping results to different targets and times.
Closing question: when you see packet loss to one hop in a traceroute, is the loss always caused by that hop? Not necessarily — some routers deprioritize ICMP, so use multiple checks to confirm the problem location.

screens.title: traceroute / tracert — discover the network path
screens.narratorSegment: Traceroute, or tracert on Windows, reveals the sequence of routers between your host and a destination. It lists each hop and the round-trip time to that hop, which helps you find exactly where latency or loss begins. For example, a typical tracert to 8.8.8.8 shows the local router, then an ISP gateway, then a border router, and finally a peering hop before the destination. When a hop shows a set of asterisks rather than times, that hop did not return a reply — this could be a router that de-prioritizes or blocks ICMP TTL-exceeded messages, a firewall, or an overloaded device. The important diagnostic step is to correlate traceroute with ping: if ping to an IP beyond the hop fails, traceroute helps decide which hop to investigate. Remember that some intermediate devices intentionally hide responses, so asterisks do not always mean an outage, but they do show where visibility drops and further investigation is needed. traceroute / tracert — discover the network path means traceroute shows each hop and the time per hop, helping you identify where along the path packets stop responding or slow down.. In practical terms, see each hop and where packets slow or stop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › traceroute / tracert
What traceroute shows
Each line is a hop. Times shown are the RTT to that hop. Traceroute helps you identify the router or hop where latency spikes or replies stop arriving. Use it after ping fails or shows high latency to localize the problem.
Interpretation tips: an asterisk means no reply from that hop; repeated asterisks across many hops may indicate filtering. Consistent high times starting at a particular hop suggest congestion at or beyond that point.
Check your assumptions
Routers can deprioritize ICMP. Use multiple tests to confirm a true outage versus reply suppression.
Example tracert output
C:\Users\User>tracert 8.8.8.8

Tracing route to dns.google [8.8.8.8]
over a maximum of 30 hops:

  1    <1 ms    <1 ms    <1 ms  router.local [192.168.1.1]
  2     2 ms     1 ms     1 ms  isp-gateway.example.com [10.0.0.1]
  3    10 ms    10 ms    11 ms  border-router.isp.com [203.0.113.1]
  4    25 ms    24 ms    25 ms  google-peering.net [142.250.x.x]
  5    24 ms    24 ms    25 ms  dns.google [8.8.8.8]

Trace complete.
Scenario: if hop 3 shows repeated timeouts while hops 4 and 5 succeed, the issue may be transient reply suppression at hop 3, not necessarily complete failure. Use traceroute results together with ping to the problematic hop to validate.

screens.title: When traceroute shows '*' — diagnosing filtered or overloaded hops
screens.narratorSegment: When traceroute shows asterisks at a particular hop, you need to interpret that absence carefully. An asterisk means the router did not return the expected TTL-exceeded or ICMP reply for that probe. Common causes include firewalls that drop these probe types, routers that de-prioritize ICMP, or a device that's overloaded and not responding to diagnostic traffic. The practical follow-up is twofold: first, run ping to the target and to intermediate hops to see where replies stop. Second, corroborate with other indicators such as whether hosts beyond the hop are reachable. If later hops respond but a middle hop does not, that often indicates deliberate filtering rather than total path failure. If all subsequent hops fail as well, the outage is likely at or after that hop. A misconception to avoid is assuming the middle hop is the service owner — often edge devices hide responses while still forwarding traffic. Your next steps should include contacting upstream support if you control no devices past that hop, or examining ACLs and firewall rules if you do. When traceroute shows '*' — diagnosing filtered or overloaded hops means missing traceroute responses reveal visibility gaps; combine traceroute with ping and host reachability checks to conclude whether filtering, overload, or outage is present.. In practical terms, how to interpret missing replies and where to go next. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Diagnosing '*' in traceroute
Stepwise diagnostic process
  1. Ping the same destination and intermediate hops to confirm reply behavior.
  2. If hops after the asterisk succeed, suspect reply suppression at that hop.
  3. Check configuration or firewall/ACLs for ICMP or TTL-exceeded filtering on devices you manage.
  4. If the hop is upstream and not under your control, document the hop and contact the provider with traceroute evidence.
Concrete example: traceroute shows asterisks at hop 4 but hops 5 and 6 respond. This pattern suggests hop 4 is not responding to traceroute probes while still forwarding traffic, meaning user connectivity beyond that hop may still be intact.
Misconception
Seeing '*' does not always mean the path is broken; it often indicates filtered diagnostic traffic.
Pro tip
Pair traceroute with ping and application checks to understand real user impact before changing network configs.
Quick reference
If later hops respond: likely filtering at the starred hop.
If subsequent hops also time out: outage starts at or after the starred hop.
Document the traceroute output and timestamps; these aid upstream support in reproducing and diagnosing the visibility gap.

screens.title: ipconfig / ifconfig / ip a — check interface configuration
screens.narratorSegment: When a user reports 'no internet', the first command to run is often ipconfig on Windows or ifconfig/ip a on Unix-like systems. These commands show the machine's network identity: IPv4 address, subnet mask, default gateway, and configured DNS servers. The chapter example shows ipconfig returning a 192.168.1.100 IPv4 address, a 255.255.255.0 mask, and a default gateway of 192.168.1.1. That tells you the host believes it is on the local subnet and knows where to send traffic outside the LAN. If ipconfig shows no IPv4 address or a link-local range only, it suggests DHCP failure or an interface problem. Always check link indicators and physical connectivity for immediate issues. A misconception to avoid is assuming the presence of an IP means full connectivity — DNS or upstream routing can still fail. In practical terms, verify ip address, subnet mask, default gateway, and dns servers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › ipconfig / ifconfig
What to check in the output
  • IPv4 Address: confirms the host's network address.
  • Subnet Mask: tells you the local subnet range.
  • Default Gateway: where packets go when the destination is outside the LAN.
  • DNS Servers: where name resolution requests are sent.
Concrete example: ipconfig output that shows a valid IPv4 address and gateway indicates the host should reach the gateway. If there is no IPv4 or only a link-local entry, investigate DHCP or physical connectivity next.
Example — Windows ipconfig
C:\Users\User>ipconfig

Windows IP Configuration

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:

   Connection-specific DNS Suffix  . : localdomain
   Link-local IPv6 Address . . . . . : fe80::xxxx:xxxx:xxxx:xxxx%xx
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.100
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.1
Scenario: if a user has an IP but cannot reach the internet, note the DNS server entries for the next check with nslookup. If the gateway is missing, focus on the local link and DHCP server.

screens.title: ipconfig /all and modern Linux alternatives
screens.narratorSegment: ipconfig /all provides extended information about the interface, including hardware MAC addresses, DHCP server and lease information, and DNS server assignments. These details help when you need to confirm which DHCP server issued the address or whether the lease is current. On Linux and Mac O S, ifconfig is historically used, but the modern recommended command is ip a or ip addr show which presents similar details in a modern format. Use these extended outputs when a simple ipconfig or ifconfig shows no IPv4 or an unexpected address. For example, the presence of a link-local IPv6 address in the sample output means the interface has a self-assigned IPv6 link-local scope, which is normal. A common misstep is skipping the /all view and missing DHCP or DNS server information that explains why name resolution or gateway assignment failed. When to run extended interface checks
Run ipconfig /all or ip a when you need to see DHCP server information, lease times, or hardware MAC addresses. These fields help you determine if DHCP assignments failed or if the machine is using wrong DNS entries.
Practical check list
  • Confirm DHCP server exists and lease is valid.
  • Check DNS server addresses for expected values.
  • Note MAC address when creating DHCP reservations or filtering rules.
Tip
If you see only a link-local or self-assigned address, prioritize DHCP and physical link checks. If DNS servers look incorrect, use nslookup with a known public server to test resolution.
Why this matters
Extended interface data often reveals configuration causes that basic checks miss, saving time when diagnosing intermittent problems.

screens.title: netstat — inspect active connections and listening ports
screens.narratorSegment: Netstat is the go-to command to inspect active TCP and UDP connections as well as ports on which the machine is listening. Running netstat -an lists addresses and numerical port numbers for each socket, letting you confirm whether a service is present and connected. For example, netstat output that shows ESTABLISHED lines indicates active connections between your host and remote endpoints. This is useful when a web server is unresponsive: netstat lets you check whether the server process is actually listening on port 80 or if connections are being made to it. A common misunderstanding is to assume netstat diagnoses application-level errors; it only reveals socket state and addresses — you still need to correlate with application logs. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › netstat — active connections
What netstat reveals
Netstat -an lists active TCP connections and UDP endpoints with numerical addresses and ports. It helps you determine whether a socket is established and whether a process is listening on an expected port.
Concrete example: if a web server is not responding, use netstat to confirm whether port 80 is in LISTEN or ESTABLISHED state. If no socket exists for port 80, the web server process may not be running or may have failed to bind the port.
Common mistake
Assuming netstat shows which process owns a socket without additional flags. Netstat shows sockets and states; process mappings can require extra options.
Practical filter
Filter results for a port to confirm specific services, for example searching for ':80' to find web server sockets.
Example output
C:\Users\User>netstat -an | find "ESTABLISHED"

  TCP    192.168.1.100:50000    172.217.160.142:443    ESTABLISHED
  TCP    192.168.1.100:50001    104.26.15.106:443      ESTABLISHED
Use such lines to identify active remote endpoints and client ports. If you see many unexpected connections, investigate for misconfigurations or unusual activity.

screens.title: nslookup / dig — diagnose DNS resolution problems
screens.narratorSegment: When a user can reach an IP address but cannot reach a hostname, DNS is the likely suspect. Use nslookup on Windows or dig on Unix-like systems to query DNS servers directly. nslookup returns the DNS server used and the resolved addresses. For instance, nslookup google. com in the chapter shows the local router acting as a resolver and returns both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. A useful technique is to explicitly query a known public DNS server, such as 8.8.8.8, to determine whether the local DNS server or the domain itself is failing. If an explicit query to 8.8.8.8 succeeds while the configured server does not, the issue is with your configured DNS server. A common mistake is not specifying an alternate DNS server when local resolution fails, which wastes time assuming the domain is down. Use nslookup to separate client-side configuration from server-side DNS failures. nslookup / dig — diagnose DNS resolution problems means nslookup and dig let you query specific dns servers to determine whether name resolution failures originate from the client configuration or the resolver.. In practical terms, verify name-to-address mappings and test different dns servers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › nslookup — DNS checks
How to isolate DNS problems
Run nslookup for the hostname. If it fails against your configured DNS, repeat the command pointing at a public resolver to see if that succeeds. A successful explicit query indicates your configured DNS is the issue; a failure across resolvers suggests a broader DNS or domain issue.
Concrete example: try nslookup www.example.com 8.8.8.8. If that returns addresses but the default nslookup does not, you know the problem lies with the configured DNS server rather than the domain itself.
Common mistake
Skipping explicit server queries and assuming the domain is down when local DNS is the problem.
Pro tip
Record the server name and address returned by nslookup to confirm which resolver responded.
Example nslookup output
C:\Users\User>nslookup google.com

Server:  router.local
Address:  192.168.1.1

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:    google.com
Addresses:  2607:f8b0:4004:80c::200e
          142.250.190.142
Use the returned server field to see whether your router or an upstream resolver answered. If the resolver is unexpectedly your router or a local appliance, that may explain failures when an upstream resolver works.

screens.title: Practical walkthrough: diagnosing DNS and connectivity
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario follows the chapter's supplied activity for diagnosing a user who cannot access www. example. com while internal apps appear slow. Start by pinging a known IP such as 8.8.8.8 to confirm basic internet reachability. If ping fails, check ipconfig /all for IPv4 address, default gateway, and DNS servers; missing or link-local addresses point to DHCP or link issues. If ping to 8.8.8.8 works but the hostname fails, run nslookup for the hostname. If nslookup fails against your configured server, explicitly query a public server like 8.8.8.8. A successful explicit query indicates your DNS server is the problem. If DNS resolves but the site is still unreachable, run tracert to see if a particular hop introduces timeouts or high latency. For slow internal applications, use netstat -an and filter for ESTABLISHED connections to identify a high connection count or unexpected endpoints. This stepwise routine minimizes unnecessary changes and leads you to the most likely component at fault. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Hands-on workflow
Step-by-step
  1. Ping a known IP such as 8.8.8.8 to confirm basic Internet reachability.
  2. Run ipconfig /all to verify IPv4, subnet mask, gateway, and DNS server assignments.
  3. Use nslookup on the problematic hostname; if it fails, query an alternate DNS server like 8.8.8.8.
  4. If DNS resolves but access fails, run tracert to find a problematic hop.
  5. For slow internal apps, run netstat -an and inspect ESTABLISHED sockets and listening ports.
Reflection: when ping 8.8.8.8 works but nslookup fails even with an explicit query to 8.8.8.8, what does that indicate? In that case both basic connectivity and the public DNS server are reachable, so the issue likely lies with your configured DNS server or the client's DNS client configuration.
Commands referenced
ping 8.8.8.8
ipconfig /all
nslookup www.example.com
nslookup www.example.com 8.8.8.8
tracert www.example.com
netstat -an | find "ESTABLISHED"
These are quick, repeatable checks that produce evidence you can use to pinpoint the fault and explain findings to others.

screens.title: ipconfig vs ifconfig vs ip a — platform differences
screens.narratorSegment: Different operating systems provide similar information with different commands. On Windows, ipconfig is the standard tool to view interface addresses, subnet masks, default gateways, and DNS servers. On older Unix-like systems, ifconfig was traditionally used to show interface addresses and flags, but modern Linux distributions favor the ip command family — typically ip a or ip addr show — which presents a more consistent and richer view. The practical consequence is to use the native command for the platform you're troubleshooting so you see the expected fields. For example, the sample ipconfig output in this chapter shows IPv4, subnet mask, and default gateway clearly. If you are working on a Linux host and use ifconfig but it is not present, ip a will be the correct choice. The misconception to avoid is assuming a Windows command exists on Unix systems; platform-appropriate commands are required. screens.narratorSegment: The chapter lists several common mistakes that junior technicians often make. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll make the command line your most reliable troubleshooting partner. The tools covered here are small, fast, and available on nearly every machine: ping for basic reachability and latency, traceroute or tracert to see the path packets take, ipconfig or ifconfig to inspect local interface settings, netstat to reveal active connections and listening ports, and nslookup or dig to validate DNS resolution. You will learn not only how to run these tools but how to read their outputs and combine them into a stepwise diagnostic approach. For example, you might start by pinging a public IP to verify basic connectivity, then run nslookup if a hostname fails, and finally use tracert to find a broken hop. These utilities give you immediate clues about source vs. resolver vs. path problems. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to pick the right command for the symptom, interpret typical outputs, and avoid common mistakes like assuming a timeout always means the host is down. Think of these tools as quick mental checks that point you where to look next.

These objectives focus on practical skills you will need as a support technician. First, you will use ping to verify IP-level reachability and to measure round-trip latency. Knowing how to interpret ping output tells you whether a host is reachable and whether packet loss or high latency exists. Second, you'll learn to read traceroute or tracert output so you can identify the network hop where packets stop responding or begin to slow down. That helps isolate routing or middlebox problems. Third, you will inspect local interface configuration with ipconfig on Windows and ifconfig or ip a on Unix-like systems to confirm IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways, and DNS servers. Fourth, you will analyze netstat output to find active TCP or UDP connections and listening ports, helping you detect whether a service is present or if unexpected connections exist. Each skill is paired with quick checks and a milestone so you can validate competency in real troubleshooting tasks.

Beyond individual commands, this chapter expects you to diagnose DNS resolution problems with nslookup or dig, and to use that result to distinguish between resolver issues and broader connectivity problems. You will practice specifying an alternate DNS server to see whether your configured DNS is the source of failure. Also, we'll practice a systematic workflow: start with ping to a known IP, check ipconfig or ifconfig for local settings, use nslookup on a hostname, then run tracert if a route problem is suspected, and use netstat when a service is unresponsive. Finally, you will learn to recognize common interpretation mistakes, such as assuming a ping timeout always means a host is down rather than ICMP being filtered. These additional skills connect commands into a repeatable diagnostic routine and reduce wasted effort during real incidents.

Ping is the most basic test for IP-level reachability. It sends ICMP Echo Request packets to a target and waits for Echo Replies. A successful sequence of replies tells you the host is reachable at the IP level and gives you round-trip times that show latency and packet loss percentages. For example, the sample ping to 192.168.1.1 returns four replies with 1 millisecond round trip times and zero packet loss; that confirms local connectivity to the gateway. A 'Request timed out' can mean several things: the host is down, an intermediate device is dropping ICMP, or a firewall blocks echo replies. Traceroute, or tracert on Windows, reveals the sequence of routers between your host and a destination. When traceroute shows asterisks at a particular hop, you need to interpret that absence carefully. An asterisk means the router did not return the expected TTL-exceeded or ICMP reply for that probe.
